(117) a. (ˈbà.dì) 'leaf' ... c. (ˈbá.ʃá)ɾú 'jaguar' d. (ˈá.wá)(ˌwɨ̀.dà) 'butterfly' ... f. (ˈɨ́.kɨ̀ʂ)(ˌtì.ɾù)wù 'they may sew' ... Example (117f) demonstrates that initial stress is not weight-sensitive in Yaminawa. Example (117g) demonstrates that secondary stress is also weight-insensitive. new_statements.quote: Primary stress in Yaminawa is word-initial. Metrical feet are left-aligned and iteratively trochaic, with no degenerate feet. Stress in Yaminawa is realized as an increase in vowel duration (vowels in stressed syllables are around 10-20 percent longer than vowels in unstressed syllables [...]). [...] Example (117f) demonstrates that initial stress is not weight-sensitive in Yaminawa. Example (117g) demonstrates that secondary stress is also weight-insensitive. [...] A small number of nouns in Yaminawa have atypical stress patterns that are not predictable. All of these roots are three or more syllables and appear to be either loans or onomatopoetic forms.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word; the word is parsed into left-aligned syllabic trochees (σˈσ)(ˌσσ).., insensitive to syllable weight, so secondary stresses fall on the 3rd, 5th.. syllables; no degenerate feet (a final odd syllable is unfooted). Stress is cued by vowel duration. Yaminawa additionally has lexical tone (H, L, HL melodies, syllable = TBU), which Neely states does not interact with stress. Faust & Loos 2002 (SLP 51, p.18) independently agree on initial prominence: 'La primera sílaba de la frase nominal es tónica'; verb roots carry accent and high tone on the first syllable (intransitive) or first two syllables (transitive).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Iterative trochaic secondary stress on odd-numbered non-initial syllables, weight-insensitive, e.g. (ˈá.wá)(ˌwɨ.dà) 'butterfly', (ˈɨ.kɨʂ)(ˌtì.ɾù)wù 'they may sew', (ˈw̃ɨ.nã)(ˌmã.ɾìʃ)(ˌtá.kũ)ĩ; in verbs with trisyllabic reduplicants secondary stress impressionistically falls on the 4th syllable (first syllable of the base) instead.
new_statements.exceptions: A small set of 3+-syllable nouns, apparently loans or onomatopoeia, have unpredictable (final) stress: [ká.pí.ɾí.ˈbà] 'boquichico' (likely Yine loan), [tá.ká.ˈɾá] 'chicken'. Reduplicated verbs have irregular secondary stress. Monosyllabic verb roots lengthen to meet bimoraicity and always take initial stress, so attraction of stress by long vowels cannot be tested.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (phonological) word; examples are citation forms of nouns and inflected verbs from the Río Sepahua dialect (ISO yaa) as spoken in Sepahua, Ucayali, Peru (Nahua/mts speakers also consulted). Tone is lexical and orthogonal to stress per the author. Note a genuine cross-source conflict: Brazilian descriptions of Jaminawa (Cruvinel 2013 MA, p.57) and of Saynáwa (Couto 2015, p.189) report FINAL primary stress; these are different communities in Acre (and Saynáwa's affiliation to Yaminawa is disputed), and neither analyses tone, so final H tone/phrase-final prominence may underlie the difference.
new_statements.identity_note: Primary statement (Neely 2019) describes the Río Sepahua dialect of Yaminawa (ISO yaa = yami1256) as spoken in Sepahua, Ucayali, Peru, with some Nahua (Yora, ISO mts, glottocode yora1241? -- Neely treats it under the blanket term Yaminawa) speakers consulted; Faust & Loos 2002 is also Peruvian Yaminahua (Purús/Yurúa SIL work). The Brazilian sources describe other communities of the Headwaters Nawa dialect complex: Cruvinel 2013 = 'Jaminawa do Brasil' (Acre: Assis Brasil, Mamoadate, Sena Madureira) and reports final stress; Couto 2015 = Saynáwa of T.I. Jamináwa do Igarapé Preto (Acre), a moribund variety whose membership in Yaminawa is disputed (Glottolog files it under yami1256 following Fleck 2013; Valenzuela & Guillaume place it in the Ucayali/Chama subgroup), also final stress. Catalog entry should be keyed to Peruvian Yaminawa (yaa) with the Brazilian discrepancy flagged.

sources.note: p.257: 'Primary stress in Yaminawa is word-initial. Metrical feet are left-aligned and iteratively trochaic, with no degenerate feet.' Stress realized as ~10-20% longer vowel; weight-insensitive (117f,g); secondary stress on odd syllables; a few 3+-syllable loans/onomatopoeia (kapiriˈba 'boquichico', takaˈra 'chicken') have unpredictable stress; reduplicated verbs impressionistically irregular in secondary stress. Language also has lexical tone (H, L, HL; TBU = syllable), p.273: 'There is no evidence for interactions between tone and stress.' Variety: Río Sepahua Yaminawa (yaa) + Nahua speake…

sources.note: Introducción, 'Fonología y símbolos ortográficos', p.18: 'No se escribe el acento. La raíz del verbo transitivo lleva acento y tono alto en las dos primeras sílabas. La raíz del verbo intransitivo lleva acento y tono alto únicamente en la primera sílaba. La primera sílaba de la frase nominal es tónica.' Repeated p.102-103 with examples [páké-] 'hacer caer' vs [páke-] 'caerse'; p.76 tonal pattern of disyllabic nouns diagnoses truncated third syllable. Accent and high tone are treated together; initial prominence.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1.2, p.189-190: 'o acento primário é predizível na última sílaba das palavras.. revelando que o acento no Saynáwa não é morfológico'; primary stress on the final syllable regardless of weight, secondary stress on non-final heavy syllables ((C)VC, (C)V:) and on alternating light syllables in 4+ syllable words; metrical (Hayes 1995) analysis with Destressing in Clash. CAUTION: Saynáwa is a moribund variety whose affiliation is disputed (Fleck 2013 lists it as Yaminawa of Brazil; Valenzuela & Guillaume place it near Shipibo/Kapanawa; speakers reject the Jamináwa label) -- not a safe prima…
